title: Duct Sealing vs. Duct Cleaning: Which Do I Need?
h1: Duct Sealing vs. Duct Cleaning: Which One Do You Need?
description: Duct cleaning removes buildup inside your ducts, while sealing fixes leaks that waste air. Learn which symptoms point to each and when a home needs both.
quick_answer: Duct cleaning removes dust and debris inside the ducts. Duct sealing closes the leaks that let conditioned air escape and pull dirty attic air in. If you see dust, debris or contamination, you likely need cleaning. If rooms are uneven, airflow is weak or bills feel high, you likely need sealing. Many attic duct systems need both.
body:
Start with the problem you notice. Dust, debris and smells usually point to cleaning. Rooms that won't cool or heat evenly, weak airflow and a system that runs and runs point to leaks and sealing. Many homes have a bit of both, because leaky ducts pull in dust that then settles inside the system.

What does duct cleaning fix?

Duct cleaning removes what's sitting inside the ducts. It helps when:

  • Dust blows out of registers when the system starts
  • You've remodeled and drywall dust got into the vents
  • Rodents or insects have been in the ductwork
  • Smoke residue or odor keeps coming back
  • There's visible buildup behind register covers

Cleaning doesn't fix leaks, and it won't change airflow much unless the ducts were badly clogged. Our air duct services cover cleaning, sealing and repair, so we can tell you which one matches the problem.

What does duct sealing fix?

Duct sealing closes gaps at joints, seams, connections and register boots. Leaky supply ducts dump cooled or heated air into the attic. Leaky return ducts pull attic air into the system, along with dust, insulation fibers and heat. Signs you may need sealing include:

  • Rooms at the end of long runs that never get comfortable
  • Weak airflow from some registers even with a clean filter
  • Upstairs rooms that stay hot on summer afternoons
  • Dust that comes back quickly even after cleaning
  • Higher energy bills without a clear reason
  • Dirt streaks around ceiling registers

Why are leaks so common in San Diego homes?

Most homes here run their ducts through the attic, where inland summer heat dries out old tape and loosens connections. Flex duct can sag, kink or slip off its fittings over time. Roof rats chew holes in it. And in older stucco tract homes, original metal ducts and later additions often meet at joints that were never sealed well in the first place.

Because the attic is hot in summer and cool on winter nights, any leak there costs you comfort in both seasons.

How do you know which one you need?

A technician can usually tell during an inspection. That includes looking inside the ducts at several points, checking connections and boots in the attic, measuring airflow at registers and looking for disconnected or crushed runs. Some jobs also include a pressure test to measure how leaky the system is.

What you noticeLikely need
Dust puffing from vents, visible debrisCleaning
Rodent droppings or odor from ventsCleaning, repair and often sealing
Uneven rooms, weak airflowSealing or repair
High bills, system runs constantlySealing, plus a system check
Dust returns quickly after cleaningSealing, especially returns

What happens during duct sealing?

Sealing starts at the places that leak most: the connection at the air handler, the return plenum, branch takeoffs and the boots where ducts meet ceiling registers. Technicians use mastic, a thick paste that hardens into a flexible seal, or foil tape rated for ducts. Regular cloth duct tape isn't used because it dries out and peels in a hot attic.

Disconnected runs get reattached with proper fittings and straps, and sagging flex duct gets supported so it doesn't pinch. In some homes, ducts with torn insulation are rewrapped or replaced so they don't sweat in summer.

After sealing, many homeowners notice stronger airflow in rooms that used to feel stuffy, and less dust settling on furniture.

When should you do both?

If the ducts are dirty and leaky, clean first and seal second. Sealing dirty ducts traps debris inside. Cleaning without sealing means attic dust starts coming back in right away.

Some ducts are past saving. Flex duct that's torn, crushed or heavily contaminated is often better replaced than cleaned and sealed. We'll show you photos and explain the options before any work starts. You can see current offers on our specials page.
faqs: Can I seal my ducts myself?

You can seal accessible joints near the air handler with mastic or foil tape rated for ducts. Avoid cloth duct tape, which fails quickly. Most attic ducts are hard to reach and easy to damage, so a professional is usually the better option.
Does duct sealing improve air quality?
Often, yes. Sealing leaky return ducts keeps attic dust, insulation fibers and odors from being pulled into the system and blown through the house.
How long does duct sealing last?

Sealing done with mastic or duct-rated materials can last many years. Tape-only repairs and connections in very hot attics may loosen sooner, so it's worth having them checked during routine maintenance.
